contributions: DeepWalk: first application of the skip-gram framework to graphs, using unbiased random walks to define node similarity
node2vec: introduces biased random walks with parameters p and q to selectively capture homophily (BFS-like) or structural equivalence (DFS-like)
Shows theoretical connection between random walk methods and implicit matrix factorization of graph transition matrices
limitations: Shallow embeddings are transductive: each node has a dedicated learned parameter vector, so new nodes appearing after training cannot be embedded without retraining. Parameters p and q are not universally optimal and depend on downstream task and graph structure, requiring grid search over values like {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}.
methods: DeepWalk generates r random walks of length L from each node, treating walks as sentences and applying the skip-gram model with negative sampling to optimize node embeddings. node2vec extends this with a second-order biased random walk where transition probabilities depend on hyperparameters p (return parameter) and q (in-out parameter), controlling whether walks explore locally (BFS-like) or globally (DFS-like). Both use negative sampling with K≈5-20 samples to avoid the O(|V|) softmax bottleneck.
results: On the Karate Club graph with p=q=1, 2D PCA projections cleanly separate the two factions without using any node labels — the instructor's group (nodes 0-8, 10-14) clusters separately from the president's group (nodes 15-33). The paper establishes that DeepWalk implicitly factorizes log(vol(G)/r * sum_t=1 to r (D^-1 A)^t D^-1) - log(b), connecting random walk methods to algebraic matrix factorization.
tldr: Shallow node embedding methods like DeepWalk and node2vec learn low-dimensional vector representations of graph nodes by treating random walks as 'sentences' and applying the skip-gram objective, with node2vec adding hyperparameters p and q to control BFS/DFS exploration trade-offs.
